item.title: Dope, 2015 - ★★★
item.description:
Ten years later Dope may be the most specifically 2015 film I have ever seen. This is an absolute time capsule that could be included in an anthropology text. ASAP Rocky has a role as an empoweringly intelligent drug-dealer, back when "stay woke" meant knowing about Obama's drone strikes. A hacker sells their drugs with Bitcoin. There is a Facebook stand-in and the Sickest Party Ever gets photos posted online. Getting into Harvard is treated as a real achievement. And the kids are obsessed with 90s music. (Partially this is because the director was a 42-year-old man who remembers the 90s, but the nostalgia was still accurate.) It represents a very, very particular kind of cool-but-not-bougie black person who absolutely loves Lakeith Stanfield and Zoe Kravitz. (She's as beautiful and wooden as ever.)

For all its extreme cultural specificity it veers off into ridiculous territory in the second half and loses a ton of steam the second that the nerd squad becomes successful drug-dealers. It feels almost insecure, like it can't just be a comedy about dorky high-schoolers so it has to throw in some violence and criminal hijinks. The dull ending and general NPR humor prevent it from taking its place alongside the great South Central comedies of the 90s that it is clearly an homage to. (Also the kid from Grand Budapest Hotel really lacks street cred.) But I remember 2015. It's not so bad to go back.

item.title: Gremlins, 1984 - ★★★
item.description:
This takes the format of a classic fairy tale: a boy is granted a magical gift with certain limits, he disregards the limits, and must set things right by using some other magical weakness. Like most fairy tales, it is somewhat predictable and way too dark for the intended kid audience. Even darker and more inexplicable than the villains is the dead Santa Claus backstory of Kate Beringer's father: who put this in the movie? The general tone is certainly mean-spirited. The original "gremlins" were unexplained errors in machinery like planes and trucks: I sense a missed opportunity here for a more subtle kind of mischief. Maybe the gremlins could have slowly brought the industrial backbone of the town to its knees over months. But that would be boring so the gremlins just rampage through town over one night.

The Spielberg tropes show up here in force--fantastic practical effects, a scene at a movie theater showing excessive veneration for cinema, and big-ass lights shining on someone's astonished face. Somehow I missed this one growing up, but its hold on Gen X childhood has mostly evaporated from younger generations. Outside of Family Guy references I don't see Gremlins staying much longer in the cultural consciousness.

item.title: Dawn of the Dead, 1978 - ★★★★½
item.description:
Lots of people today criticize the Romero Dead movies for the slow zombies. Cheesy, not scary, not as visceral as the new-generation fast zombies the 28 __ Later films introduced. But the slow zombie is a taste for the refined horror palate. Dawn of the Dead is the best zombie movie ever made because it embraces the slow zombie and turns it into a piercing critique of capitalism. Like capital, zombies don't need to quickly overwhelm you to kill you. They just advance inexorably, never sleeping or stopping, and just wait for you to make a mistake. At least you get to have fun while waiting for your lonely death.

All films about the apocalypse are also films about capitalism, but Dawn really grasps the fact that both are dangerous because they are so enjoyable. The apocalypse, like a well-stocked mall, gives you everything you could ever want. Americans in the 70s already yearned to gun down hordes of faceless urbanites, feeding their bloodlust with revenge movies like Dirty Harry and Death Wish. In the beginning of Dawn one vicious cop gets in on the action a bit early and starts wasting civilians. This gets him killed by his fellow cops. Poor guy: if he just waited 12 hours, he could have all the violence he ever wanted.

The violence really does get fun for our leftover band of protagonists. In the middle of the film the zombie killing becomes downright ecstatic. Scott Reiniger's character Roger starts whooping and hollering as he guns them down. Romero understands that every single man who has ever lived has fantasized about a mass shooting or doomsday scenario, where the best outcome is he gets to be a hero, and the second-best outcome is he gets to kill people without consequences. The typical survivalist fantasy of the apocalypse assumes our decadent lifestyles will get simplified into the essentials through privation. Dawn of the Dead takes the end of the world as a chance to maximize our excess and kill us with it. The Good Life--living in a mall, shooting zombies, wearing sick-ass fur coats--curdles into a hell that closely resembles 70s American life. It ends with a hell that probably resembles 2020s American life: rival gangs breaking into paradise and allowing the long-clamoring hordes to invade. This film is a microcosm of American history and a prediction of its future. It is brilliant.

item.title: Civil War, 2024 - ★★★½
item.description:
Political theorist Benjamin Studebaker made the point in 2024 that the memory of the 20th century essentially precludes all attempts at political violence in the West. Holocaust movies, WWII video games, footage of the trenches in Verdun and the Somme: these drill into us the idea that any ideas about changing the political status quo outside of legal tweaks inevitably lead to mass death and hell. Political ideology is the realm of fanatics. So how could the US actually slip into a civil war? It happened once, so it isn't inconceivable in the way something like a Communist revolution seems truly impossible here. But 1865 was a long time ago.

Alex Garland, an Englishman, doesn't even touch this question, which does seem prudent. But he also doesn't portray, say, the innocent civilians whose lives are torn apart by the war, as might be expected for a bog-standard "war is hell" movie. Instead he follows journalists.

Narratively this weakens Civil War tremendously. Photojournalists have not mattered in a long time, maybe not since Vietnam (although Vice had a fun thing going in the 2010s.) They fulfill no function at all today, when constant videos from warzone civilians and soldiers and drones filter onto Reddit and Telegram. Speaking of drones, they are nowhere to be seen: as shown by his Iraq film, Garland seems to be stuck in a style of war now 20 years out of date. While Kirsten Dunst brings a level of grit to an underwritten protagonist, her young protegee Jessie just comes across as super annoying. While Garland has made public statements about this film trying to emphasize the importance of journalists, it comes across more as a satire of these journalists. Jessie in particular seems like a social climber (obvious for any media figure) and bloodthirsty (less obvious).

But Jessie's simultaneous desire to see violence and desire to gain status unlock an alternate reading of the film. In this light, Garland's decision to focus on journalists in the middle of a civil war makes perfect sense because the journalists are the vector of the media that would cause political violence. Eventually all the anti-war messages backfire. Eventually all the HD drone footage showing Ukrainians and Russians getting blown to mushy bits while EDM music blares starts to tempt the nihilistic young men of the West, and the politicians willing to whore for their votes. Eventually the unthinkable becomes inevitable. We will march into the next civil war not out of duty or ideology but boredom. Already we see this in the noxious AI videos championing a destructive war with Iran. Baby wants blood, and the journalists will both feed us the snuff footage and engorge themselves on it. If that is what Garland intended, then Civil War might be very profound indeed, rather than out-of-touch.

item.title: The Tenant, 1976 - ★★½
item.description:
The Tenant is quite obviously the weakest of Roman Polanski's "Apartment trilogy", the other 2 being Rosemary's Baby and Repulsion. Nothing unites other than a general feeling of paranoia in a crowded city apartment, a theme quite prevalent amidst the rising crime of the late 60s and 70s. The previous two films bordered on shtick (as with the neighbor couple in Rosemary's Baby), but enjoyed strong leading performances from Catherine Deneuve and Mia Farrow. The Tenant suffers from the catastrophic choice to cast Polanski himself in the lead. A charisma void who mutters through most of his lines, his character Trelkovsky's meekness is mostly exasperating. Unable to sell the Kafkaesque atmosphere, Trelkovsky's descent into madness becomes comedic, especially in the moment when he decides to take up cross-dressing.

The script remains fairly strong, which may explain why some it has been reevaluated since its release. But I have to side with the contemporary critics: this is a scattered and uninspired film. The score resorts to generic strings, Isabelle Adjani shows up with nothing to do, and the "shocking" twist ending is as predictable as you can get. This film would be Polanski's last before he drugged and raped a 13-year-old, then fled to Europe. It immediately followed his greatest triumph, Chinatown. The unmistakable vibe of an egomaniac growing sloppy pervades The Tenant. As with Woody Allen, the directorial urge to cast yourself as a loser who nonetheless scores beautiful young babes (Adjani was 20 during the filming of The Tenant) foreshadows the inevitable fall.

item.title: Ball of Fire, 1941 - ★★★★
item.description:
Ball of Fire may have one of the more insane comedy premises you'll ever see. It is also charmingly analog, completely impossible in today's networked day and age. We don't write encyclopedias anymore, and anyone writing an encyclopedia wouldn't need to find a streetwise singer to give them tips on slang. (I am not sure how much of this slang is real and how much is made up, a la Heathers.) And unfortunately, there aren't many mansions full of charmingly spacey professors in prime New York City real estate anymore. America used to be a country, we've really declined in some ways since 1941. There is a mob plot thrown in there too. Honestly, it makes Bringing Up Baby look like a restrained Oscar bait drama. But the completely ridiculous concept does manage to give us a genuinely fresh odd couple: a sheltered professor (played by Gary Cooper, who does his best to not seem like a chad) and a burlesque performer.

It shows confidence by the great Howard Hawks to commit to this bit. Fortunately he has Barbara Stanwyck on his side, and as I've worked through more 30s and 40s films, I've realized Stanwyck is one of the great Golden Age performers, maybe the most distinctive and consistently good actress of the era. Ball of Fire is another notch on her sparkly, shiny belt.

item.title: Leviathan, 2014 - ★★★★½
item.description:
At the end of the Book of Job, after punshing his faultless servant with untold suffering God decides to make everything better. He restores Job's health and riches, grants him long life, and even lets him get a new family. Forget about the children you lost, here are some new ones! The abrupt finale resembles a Hollywood feel-good story, a huge tonal shift from the philosophical, bitterly pessimistic narrative.

In fact many scholars believe this ending was tacked onto the original story by later authors, a fan-fiction coda to settle an underwise unsettling meditation on the nature of suffering. In the original, the theory goes, the book ends with God's answer to Job: you cannot understand the world, and you will accept what is given to you. Andrey Zvyagintsev restores this original ending in Leviathan, named for the great fish that God describes to Job, a sign of his terrifying power. "Behold, the hope of him is in vain."

Bleak? This movie is set in remote northern Russia, where plinking bottles with Kalashnikovs is the main entertainment. One is reminded of an anecdote from "Traumazone", where a man in the rural USSR describes his average day as driving around with his friends from liquor store to liquor store to find vodka. Many in Russia panned this film for playing into all the stereotypes: drunk Russians, corrupt government, fatalistic philosophy. The irony is that this kind of brutally uncompromising work is what has always appealed to non-Russians. The world doesn't read Dostoevsky and Solzhenitsyn for their smoked herring recipes.

I can only complain that I was misled by many into believing this film would have a Killdozer. No such Killdozing happens. The Killdozer incident took place in America, where people are still deluded enough to challenge the government with an armored bulldozer. That's American can-do spirit and ingenuity at work. In Russia, the alcoholic main character, Nikolai, cannot muster up the time or the capital to challenge all the forces humiliating and degrading him. He must shuffle off to prison. Might he return in a few years redeemed, like Raskolnikov in Crime and Punishment? They've already built a church on his house. In Russia, bulldozer destroy you. What can Nikolai say? What does an audience, watching his suffering, expect him to say? Job answered the Lord: "I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes."

item.title: Zelig, 1983 - ★★★★
item.description:
Zelig embodies the pain of the comedian, the sad clown who makes everyone laugh by adapting himself for everyone else. Woody Allen, usually such a large (sometimes unwanted) presence in his own movies, takes a backseat as Leonard Zelig. While ostensibly the star he rarely talks. We get very few of his classic neurotic rants or quips; he is mostly seen in newsreels or photographs. In fact the entire movie sidelines the jokes for a premise more intellectual than engaging. The chameleon man may represent a broader social issue--the ultimate conformist in a conformist society--but in typical Woody fashion, this "illness" is individualized and treated with therapy. Zelig conforms because he yearns for approval. Recognizing the problem psychologically lets him solve it; with the help of Mia Farrow's love, the movie ends happily. In Allen's world, analysis conquers all.

It comes at an opportune moment in his career. He probably could not have made such a singular movie, with his particular interest in 1920s pop culture and lack of entertainment, earlier in his career. He probably would not have had such an eye for detail later in his career, when he sped up his production schedule to one movie a year. Zelig is meticulous, not a word often associated with Allen. They created a mockumentary the hard way, without digital technology. The newsreel footage looks insanely authentic, and he captures highly specific aspects of 20s culture beyond the stereotypical flappers. You can tell Woody wants to impress. Meant to be dissected more than watched, Zelig strains a bit for prestige but mostly achieves it.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Die My Love, 2025 - ★★★
item.description:
Madness is an ugly and deeply embarrassing state. We often use the benign word "cringe", but true embarrassment is worrying, a state of dread produced by terror about what will happen next. Die My Love puts Robert Pattinson and Jennifer Lawrence through the paces of weirdness--they crawl on the floor, jump through glass windows, and commit random acts of violence. It all remains beautiful rather than ugly, and strange rather than embarrassing.

Lawrence really commits to her role, but her underling persona remains a defiant and resilient woman who keeps her cool in the face of suffering. Compare this to the all-time performance by Gena Rowlands in the film that clearly inspired this one, A Woman Under the Influence. Rowlands portrays a crumbling soul, someone who veers so close to annihilation that the film almost feels invasive, like we shouldn't be watching this woman deteriorate. Die My Love does not reach that kind of vulnerability. I actually think this comes down more to director Lynne Ramsay, who reportedly gave little active instruction to her actors on set. With some guidance this might have been an enormously affecting movie. Instead it flirts with depression without surrendering to it, which makes it more hopeful and less true.

item.title: Nadja, 1994 - ★★
item.description:
The 90s indie boom produced a lot of idiosyncratic classics with striking visuals and a cool, music-video aesthetic. Nadja is not one of them. Despite being financed by David Lynch (who has an unmemorable cameo) and featuring some amazing needle drops from Portishead's first album Dummy, this film really adds nothing new to the often-told Dracula story while also being more boring than the original, Victorian-era novel. Elina Lowesohn is, sorry, a disaster in the title role. The awesomely-named Galaxy Craze doesn't fare much better as Lucy.

The movie lacks the budget and vision to go for something truly weird and surreal, but it also refuses to bend to any commercial impulses, stubbornly sticking to interminable static shots and pointless montages. It reminds me of sharing a cigarette with a slow-talking European "concept artist" outside some club at 3 AM. You think they might be interesting at first, but after 20 minutes of droning you just want to go back inside. Very cool that you never sold out, but please stop talking. We're not listening.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: The Mastermind, 2025 - ★★★
item.description:
Kelly Reichardt has a gift for understatement. In movies like First Cow and Showing Up, that understatement allows her to delicately view relationships between people without sentimentality or judgment. As a film focused on individual alienation, though, The Mastermind brings its understatement to the level of opaqueness. It would work quite well as a short story, but as a film it lacks interiority. I simply do not know what is going on with Josh O'Connor's JB. His alienation does not feel specific to the character, but stands in for a kind of general 70s American anomie. Compare this to Le Samourai, which influenced her, and which showed a character who self-consciously aestheticized his own detachment, in the manner of a Paul Schrader protagonist (or, weirdly for a movie about an assassin, in a proto-incel way). That is much more understandable than O'Connor's aw-shucks naturalism.

The plottiness also worked against Reichardt's style. Instead of enjoying the slapstick heist elements, I found them distracting. The best scene in the movie recalls First Cow. It features O'Connor hiding his stolen paintings in a pig stall. This plays exactly to Reichardt's strengths of careful observation. Otherwise I found the collision of heist movie and slow cinema to be unsuccessful.

item.title: The Brainiac, 1962 - ★★
item.description:
The insane title and ridiculous makeup might make you think the Brainiac is some sort of delirious camp horror classic, but the film largely plays it safe. Despite a tight 80-minute runtime, the setup is very repetitive: the eponymous Baron hypnotizes women, shape-shifts, and sucks out their brains. In between these slow-paced horror scenes there is interminable discussion about comets. Just endless astronomy lessons. This is what you get for putting scientists in your movie!

Had this movie come out in the 70s and had a slightly larger budget, it might have been a psychosexual gonzo thriller. However, outside of the striking opening set in 1661, this B-movie fails to distinguish itself from more inventive horror films of the era.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Sleepaway Camp, 1983 - ★★★
item.description: To stay competitive in a crowded slasher market, you have to get creative. Sleepaway Camp has a pretty similar setup to Friday the 13th. The plot--children getting knocked off mysteriously at camp--is pure formula. The characters are mostly stock 80s archetypes: bitchy bully, dreamy jock, quiet shy girl. So Sleepaway Camp innovates in the margins. The cafeteria cook is an unabashed pedophile: you don't see that too often. One character, Aunt Martha, wandered onto set from a Liza Minnelli musical. And of course there's the ending: strange mostly in how it luxuriates in its own strangeness. The twist, which probably started as a cheap trick to prevent you from guessing the killer, reframes the whole movie (for some) as a real statement on gender. That gives Sleepaway Camp way too much credit.

item.title: Wes Craven's New Nightmare, 1994 - ★★★★
item.description:
Is it possible to actually care about events you know to be fiction? The 90s saw an extended cinematic experiment in balancing emotional connection with a film and the meta knowledge that you are just watching a movie. Usually you do this with a wry, ironic, smirking kind of tone, like in Pulp Fiction or Scream. In New Nightmare Wes Craven tries to take Freddie Krueger fairly seriously--more seriously than in previous Nightmare on Elm Street films, which were not actually meta. He does this by embedding the meta aspect deep into the film's structure and plot. Characters don't just know the tropes of horror films: the script literally predicts future events, and actors who played movie characters play actors who are forced to become movie characters.

Everything holds together logically because of one assumption: fiction can create its own reality, one more significant than the "real" world. Already in 1994 many people lived their emotional lives in make-believe worlds of media (remember Society of the Spectacle was published all the way back in 1967). Of course media devices have only grown more omnipresent, addictive, and immersive since then. We care more about media than ever, to our obvious detriment. New Nightmare just uses a simple supernatural trick (the metaphor of Freddie) to make a deadly monster stand in for an emotional investment in fiction. Craven took this much further in the Scream series, making every Scream sequel revolve around copycat fans who recreate the Ghostface murders from a previous film.

Now, the plot of New Nightmare frames this process as fiction keeping a leash on our brutal, primal drives: the entity called Freddie is contained so long as new Nightmare on Elm Street movies come out. This resembles the sublimation theory that video games reduce crime by allowing us to act out violent acts virtually. Here the Spectacle is understood as a prophylactic cure, a numbing solution to prevent harmful actions from spilling into the real world. Does Wes Craven support the Spectacle? Maybe. Yet who is Freddie killing? Actors, fans, and collaborators: people intimately connected with the Nightmare series. The nightmare of modern media is that the franchises will never end: we are trapped inside the mind of Freddie, or more accurately the mind of Wes Craven. Eventually this will kill us, but Freddie will endure. He has even outlasted Wes Craven.

item.title: The Secret Agent, 2025 - ★★★★
item.description:
From Brazil, a country still pulsing with life, we get a film that finally marries style with thoughtful substance. Unlike the Cargo Cult Arthouse being made on the dead old continent of Europe, The Secret Agent contains real historical memory, real political injustice, and real tragedy. The sex scenes are actually sexy. The violence is actually shocking. Many things that irk me about modern films are still here: a too-long runtime, a muddle middle. But Kleber Mendonca does so many little things well with this movie that it is hard to dislike the finished whole. One example: has anyone Hollywood movie recently equaled the casting in this? This film is a delight of strange faces and unusual character actors. If we compare this to One Battle After Another, then Tania Maria's Dona Sebastiana equals or surpasses Benicio del Toro's Sergio as the protector of a band of political refugees.

One mark of quality: it made several unusual moves that unsettled me at first, but which I later came to appreciate. The Hairy Leg segment? It seems incredibly bizarre and unnecessary in the moment, but when I learned the history behind this (that it was a real life incident used by a newspaper to cover up police brutality) I realized it was brilliant. Similarly, I groaned at first when I saw Wagner Moura playing Armando's son, but his performance is so distinct and so contemporary, twitchy and polite and slightly false and so different from his soulful 70s father, that the choice to put Moura on double duty became clear. Good films should take calculated risks. We as viewers will usually find them weird at first. That's good! A film which doesn't unsettle us will be forgotten.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Re-Animator, 1985 - ★★★½
item.description: Disgusting, mean-spirited, quite fun. You got to appreciate older grindhouse films like Re-Animator that were made by true sickos with a sense of craft. This comes from the glory days of practical effects, the mid-1980s, and all the gore and makeup have a charming grossness that toes the line between comedy and horror in the manner of Evil Dead. Jeffrey Combs plays Herbert West with an amoral mania that feels very true to life for an actual mad scientist (I have met many Herbert Wests in Silicon Valley who would gladly test serums on zombies and steal dad cats if they could.) There is little in the way of social or genre commentary here, which prevents it from reaching the heights of Brian Yuzna's later film Society. But Re-Animator commits to the blood as a form of comic expression: it is a canonical splatter film, transgressive in its decadence.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: The Beast, 2023 - ★★½
item.description:
The Beast is an example of a common trend we see now that I call Cargo Cult Arthouse. These movies look good, utilize cool actors, and talk about Topics of the Day like alienation, AI, and online culture. They feature elliptical narratives and some symbolism. They have all the trappings of a serious work of art. But they are hollow and empty. They are devoid of life.

Falseness often enters the narrative to ruin sincere moments before they can develop. Why does Gabrielle speak in such a way to the strange Louis after an earthquake? Why is this version of Elliot Rodger also cool enough to smoke cigs while leaning back stylishly? Why was this man even cast to play Elliot Rodger when he cannot muster any darkness in his eyes? But the film, in a common tactic today, also uses meta tricks to ruin sincere moments itself. A scene where Lea Seydoux is stalked in a house is intercut, in a thuddingly obvious fashion, with a previous scene that undercuts it. Cargo Cult Arthouse films are zombies. They try to convince us that a lack of life is an asset because we live in a time of zombies, of undead algorithms and undead companies and undead politicians. We do not need undead movies like The Beast.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Carrie, 1976 - ★★★★
item.description:
The pig blood prom prank in Carrie remains, to this day, the single meanest act ever committed in cinema. Amon Goeth in Schindler's List does not approach the hateability of Nancy Allen's Chris. (When she is killed, the entire theater began clapping and cheering.) For all the 70s cheesiness this movie still works because it preys on the universally horrifying experience that is high school. Brian dePalma also understood the craft of filmmaking so well that the prom scene, despite being spoiled on the poster and immediately becoming something of a meme, remains as good a signature scene as any in horror.

Piper Laurie's religious fanatic mother doesn't land quite as well, but the movie is stripped-down enough to never get bogged down in anything too tedious. The simplicity of it approaches fable: Carrie is not a complicated experience, but it is very effective.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Interview with the Vampire, 1994 - ★★★½
item.description:
Most of us have lived our entire lives assuming certain universally acknowledged truths about vampires: that they are rich, bisexual, and very sad. Imagine my surprise when I learned that Interview with the Vampire invented most of these truths! Well, the 70s book series did. On film, Tony Scott's The Hunger certainly introduced some of these conventions (with David Bowie and Catherine Deneuve, no less), and Bram Stoker's Dracula gave vampires a new level of sumptuous seriousness, but Interview with the Vampire solidified a new kind of vampire. While Brad Pitt can tend towards one-note mopeyness, the movie truly nails the kind of postmodern ennui we associate with the endlessly wealthy, endlessly acquisitive undead. How suitable this approach was for the 90s, for the End of History, for the listless generation that saw no future forward but consumption. Not for nothing that it is Christian Slater, a totemic Gen X actor, who begs Brad Pitt's Louis to turn him into a vampire too.

Here, too, we can see the origins of much conspiracy theory. Along with Eyes Wide Shut, it trafficks in the idea of a cosmopolitan, ancient elite. While Dracula existed alone, Louis learns that other vampires have embedded themselves in the heart of Belle Époque Paris. (Although I had to laugh at the Paris scenes being set during the Prussian siege in 1870, when most Parisians were probably not enjoying theatrical horror shows.) Like our own jet-setting rulers, the vampires ask for absolute devotion from their new charge, and punish him by punishing a child. Kirsten Dunst turns in the best performance of the film as the young Claudia, and while she may not have the scene-stealing quality of the reliably unhinged Tom Cruise, the movie lives and breathes with her. Now I'm not going to explicitly compare this to something like Epstein, but I'll only say that Interview with the Vampire still resonates past the melodrama and homoeroticism because it portrays the aspirations of the elite so well: to be sad, to feed on others, and to never die.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Frankenstein, 2025 - ★★
item.description:
To understand how lazy and unoriginal this latest Frankenstein is, consider an early scene where Victor Frankenstein demonstrates his reanimation experiments to his shocked colleagues. Frankenstein invented so many tropes that it can be hard for every single scene not to feel like a retread, but consider the style of this one: melodramatic overacting, thudding orchestral cues, cliche after cliche in the dialogue, and blatant anachronism. (This 1818 novel is set in 1857, but also displays lightbulbs and 20th-century-style toilets, along with some very un-Victorian screaming and histrionic shrieking. The only thing historically accurate about this film are the costumes.) Add in some video-game quality CGI, especially in the North Pole-set beginning, and you get a comic book movie aiming for prestige by association with a classic novel.

What happened to Guillermo del Toro? The man who once made delicate, brilliant fables like Pan's Labyrinth has spent too much time making action slop like Hellboy and Pacific Rim (both superior to this one). Mia Goth is spectacularly miscast, despite her beautiful dresses, and Oscar Isaac, unfortunately, does everything his director asks of him. There is a great demand right now among the cool cinephiles for art that is weird or "feral" or "unhinged," and this unfeeling product uses its beautiful young actors, all with indie film bonafides, to trick them into mistaking melodrama for transgression. Nosferatu wasn't great either, but at least it featured Eggers' trademark attention to detail. This movie sticks to formulas: Del Toro's formula of a woman falling in love with an inhuman creature, Hollywood's formula of terrible-looking effects, and the current formula of injecting classic literature with tasteless sex and howling actors to capture the romantasy market (I expect no less from Wuthering Heights later this year). The present is artless and ugly enough; no need to slather that ugliness onto the past.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Resurrection, 2025 - ★★½
item.description:
"Chat, generate a feature film for me that compares cinema to dreaming. Make 6 segments that each match a different cinematic look in your training set. The film should move through the 20th century, so make the first part look like a silent film, the second part like a noir movie, the third part like a Kim Ki-Duk film, the fourth part like a Hirokazu Kore-eda movie, the fifth part like a Wong Kar-Wai movie, and the sixth part like a video game. Color-grade each segment accordingly. Use wax as a metaphor. Overall, make it feel like a Tarkovsky movie.

Now generate a list of possible titles that sound epic, transcendent, and oneiric."

Here’s a spread of title ideas, grouped by register rather than by concept, so you can feel which temperature fits the project.
-The Sleep of Cinema
-The Soft Century
-Resurrection
-A History of Images While Asleep
-Soft Light

This is a strong conceptual spine—quietly ambitious in a way that suits the filmmakers you’re invoking.

"Thanks. I like Resurrection."
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Glorious, 2022 - ★★
item.description:
To those who support the hauntology, "nothing ever happens and all recent history looks the exact same" thesis, I present the counter-argument. Only three years later, you can instantly spot Glorious as a COVID film. Witness the braindead and overly heightened color grading. See the uncomfortably constrained shooting locations, borne not out of artistic invention but quarantine necessity. Feel the squirming sense of "Look, we didn't WANT to shoot a movie in a rest stop, but that's all we could work with!" While the film was released before generative AI models hit the mainstream, the script is so vacuous and circular that one wonders if the writers had access to some unreleased GPT model.

Here is a script without the easygoing texture of conversation or banter, but without enough new ideas (or budget) to actually Make Things Happen minute to minute. A favorite quote of mine from an exec at Pixar is that "a movie isn't one idea, it's thousands of ideas." Glorious has about 4 ideas, and between the 4 scenes where something happens, it fills its remaining (and mercifully short) 79 minutes with pointless chatter. Lead Ryan Kwanten lacks charisma (although it would take a very gifted actor to have charisma with a disembodied voice, a la Joaquin Phoenix in Her), and has to chart a path from an extremely tired inciting incident (his girlfriend broke up with him) to an extremely tired finale (he is actually a bad guy). Along the way they sprinkle in lots of gore for the horror movie sickos. This is a COVID-era film, all right, with all the unappealing fixings.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: One Battle After Another, 2025 - ★★★★
item.description:
We will repeat the 60s and 70s until we learn from them. So yes, One Battle After Another actually takes place in the 1970s, but with cell phones. Bands of revolutionaries are not running around knocking off banks today unless Palantir and their handlers decided they want it to happen. The only scenes that really resemble Life Today are the ones dealing with Leo DiCaprio's Bob Ferguson and his daughter, probably because Paul Thomas Anderson knows a bit more about raising a child than attempting to overthrow the government. (These are also the funniest scenes.)

But politically we would all like to return to the 70s. The action scenes flatter all sides. We on the left would prefer the right-wing opposition to be battle-hardened white supremacists, as it would take some heat off our own history of largely self-inflicted failures. (Most leftists are just Bob Ferguson, but without the violent past and marksmanship.) The right would enjoy facing lefties like Perfidia, as it would justify the police state they hope to build and all the Punisher tattoos and "wolves, sheep, and sheepdog" T-shirts they get. The most consistent theme of One Battle After Another, however, lies in the old chestnut that all politics is sexual perversion. I should note that I wrote a screenplay with the exact same message and was critiqued for it, so you can to to hell, Page Screenwriting Awards.

That covers the political side. As a movie, One Battle After Another is visceral, frequently funny, and (like most movies today) a little too long. All the writers exclusively making this a political film are missing the fact that this movie is fun. That is why it's popular. We're not doing ultra-serious anymore: that's very 2018. Even Sean Penn, a guy without a working sense of humor, works well because he is so far up his own ass that his performance becomes unserious, and therefore perfect. Have fun with politics: shoot that machine gun over your pregnant belly. It's a good message for our time.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: The Wind Will Carry Us, 1999 - ★★★½
item.description:
Abbas Kiarostami apparently either makes truly brilliant movies with engaging plots and memorable finales (Close-Up, Where is the Friend's House) or extremely slow existentialist staring contests (Taste of Cherry). The Wind Will Carry Us approaches the latter category, but it does have some advantages over the dull Taste of Cherry. First, the turtle. The scene with the turtle could be an award-winning short film on its own. Second, the scene in the cave where the titular poem is quoted. Third, the many landscape shots of cars driving through the Iranian countryside, which he also exploited to great effect in Where is the Friend's House. Only Tarkovsky has more effectively used images of wind blowing through grass more effectively. Fourth, the incredible shot of Behzad Dorani shaving while using the camera lens as a mirror. The minor pleasures in this film pile up.

Still, I have a congenital allergy to artists telling me to leave the city, slow down, and enjoy the little things. It doesn't matter if the messenger is an acclaimed director or a gray-bearded Zarathustra emerging from his lair, I do not and will never accept the Word. Orangutans live solitary lives; chimps and humans live in troops, and we kill each other to be on top. Do not lecture me for my nature. Thankfully there was a Tolstoy-esque doctor at the end who gives our phone-addled protagonist a ride on his motorcycle, and this generous man of society preaches the film's message without being preachy.

Kiarostami has always been preoccupied with image and reality, and here the city-dweller life is equated with the filmic image, the Form, while village life embodies reality. Well, then, why do villagers spend so much time yapping? Get me back to Tehran, don't let me hear the old men chit-chatting around their tea for a moment longer.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Doctor X, 1932 - ★★★½
item.description: For all the salacious pre-Code material--cannibalism, disfigurement, prostitution--featured in Doctor X, the movie doesn't strike you as very horrifying. It bears more resemblance to those talky 1950s sci-fi films with aliens and experiments. Other pre-Code movies take a more daring attitude to their subject matter. The star here is instead the color cinematography, done in two-color Technicolor. While less realistic than the later three-strip process, the result looks undeniably daring. Retro film fans should give some more love to the vivid shots in Doctor X, and contemporary directors could find some new inspiration.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: The Draughtsman's Contract, 1982 - ★★★
item.description:
Plenty of filmmakers use "period pieces" as an excuse to put modern characters in old costumes. They wrap essentially contemporary dialogue with a few "Dear me"s and "certainly not"s to give it an old-timey patina. Not Peter Greenaway. It remains recognizable as his in its painterly visual style, its preoccupation with immoral sex and female revenge, and near-constant dialogue. (For a filmmaker with such visual flair, he loves to have his characters fill up the time with talking.) But I find his trademark pleasures smothered a bit under all the lace and Baroque music. The late 1600s were a very weird, very mannered time. Men wore lipstick, feathered hats, and truly enormous wigs. Greenaway's meticulous fidelity to that era made me feel constrained, like I was stuck wearing an uncomfortable costume in a very stuffy dinner party.

Some call this Greenaway's most approachable film, and I suppose that's partially true. It doesn't have the formal experimentation of his later works. Technically, it is a murder mystery. But the murder doesn't take place until halfway through the film: before that, it really does follow a draftsman (sorry I'm not British, I don't say "draughtsman") making drafts. The slow pace and deliberate camera work is also not enlivened by the same creative lighting seen in films like Drowning by Numbers.

Greenaway originally produced this for Channel 4, so he was working within the tradition of British TV period pieces. There is thus a certain adherence to tropes that was unavoidable for a first-timer director. He still made this movie his by turning up the historical accuracy, turning up the cynicism, and adding plenty of explicit sex. But I prefer his later works, where he has free rein to pursue all his obsessions without the wigs and petticoats.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: The Thin Man, 1934 - ★★★★
item.description:
Nick and Nora, never equalled, are pure delight on camera. A more aspirational couple for the city-dweller hardly exists, unless you are a doctor specializing in liver failure. It bears little resemblance to real-world crime and crime-solving, but The Thin Man takes the attitude that life should be fun, beautiful, and interesting, and missing wealthy women are nothing if not interesting. That is how Nick and Nora avoid some sort of horrible fate of French-style ennui, two rich people who have nothing but each other's company and grow to hate that company. If only all our yuppie couples could have a private investigator side-hustle, instead of starting Etsy businesses or joining nonprofit boards.

A good relationship needs some life energy, some jouissance, something you don't get from yachting or golf. Nick and Nora certainly have it. Nick also has something rare among the rich, which is courage. Despite his louche alcoholic persona, he reacts with nerves of steel to being threatened with a gun. Revealing the killer at a fancy dinner party and then punching said killer after he tries to shoot you? Cold move. This film has a Big Sleep-style impossible plot with tons of interchangeable names like Wynant, Jorgenson, and MacCauley. The names were probably chosen to sound good when spit out at 100 mph by William Powell, and in that respect they serve their purpose. The plot fades with memory, but the cocktails, the dog, and Myrna Loy's facial expressions remain.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Broadcast News, 1987 - ★★★★
item.description:
James L. Brooks created the ultimate yuppie love story in Broadcast News, one which is still relevant to the present-day strivers who descend from the original specimens of the 1980s. Every girlboss can see herself (or wants to see herself) in Holly Hunter's Jane, a woman whose commitment to her work represents one possible approach to the yuppie lifestyle. She is talented and optimistic; Albert Brooks' Aaron is talented and cynical; William Hurt's Tom is untalented and optimistic. (Untalented and cynical is a tough combination for your career; this movie has too much cheer to focus on the losers with those traits.) Clearly we can see that optimism and belief in the Company Mission take you further than talent or hard work; this is why Aaron does the worst and Tom does the best. Where does romance come in, again?

For the yuppie, the career is love. All their life force is poured into the work, leaving nothing no erotic charge left for outsiders. Those who they love mostly benefit from standing in the splash zone of work. The love a yuppie feels towards a work lover is a side effect of the work, not the lover. Tom does well at work and makes Jane feel good, so she loves him for a time. Aaron does not do well at work and brings up troublingly realistic notions about news media to Jane, so she cannot love him. In the end, though, Jane comes to her signature realization: she really does love the work, not Tom. An older movie might see her realize that work must come second to love, and go for either Tom or Aaron.

But Brooks is that rarest of screenwriters: a smart one. He understands the yuppie, and so she chooses neither. At the end Jane has a "boyfriend." As if he'll last. Aaron and Tom, by contrast, do get married, but we let men "have it all," which is another way of saying we don't care if they love their wives so long as they make money for them. Poor Jane is not given that bargain. But it means her love for work is pure. She must sacrifice for it, unlike those clueless men. She knows what it means to live for your career. She embodies the great love story of our time: When a Woman Loves a Job.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Eddington, 2025 - ★★★★½
item.description:
Eddington was the signature film of 2025 because, unlike most movies being made today, it accurately captures the feeling of being alive right now. It captures the feeling of living through screens, of being upset and confused with the world around you, of spending time and energy on inane squabbles. Crucially, though, it also recognizes that this feeling doesn't matter to the greater world. There is nothing there. Most films come at this brutal reality from one side or another: they try to capture meaning by placing their stories in some other world--the past, a fantasy or sci-fi world, or some cinematic version of Now--that does matter, or they try to capture the contemporary Moment by imbuing current artifacts like social media or smartphones with meaning.

Eddington, alone, seems to recognize what Matt Gasda said in his play "Dimes Square": we are living through the dumbest time in human history. Call this movie cynical or nasty, say it depicts both sides as stupid, criticize its rushed and unrealistic ending. That is our reality. The single best depiction of what it is like to live in the 2020s comes in the scene where Joaquin Phoenix barges into a fancy party in the middle of the pandemic and confronts his bitter rival, Pedro Pascal's mayor, while Katy Perry blasts in the background. We live in unserious times, so we need unserious movies. There is no way out presented. There is a future, but it is not for us humans. It is a data center in the desert. That is how we forget all the insane things we collectively did in 2020, the year where we all lost our minds. We will build a nonhuman mind because thinking, caring, believing leads to pointless slaughter, a gunfight where you can't see your enemies.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Baby Doll, 1956 - ★★★★
item.description:
If I watched Baby Doll in 1956, I would find it dirty, suggestive, and rather arousing. Watching it in 2025, I feel the exact same way. Condemned at the time for its controversial sexual themes, the movie has aged so well that Nicole Kidman starred in a sexy movie from 2024 with almost the same title. A 19-year-old girl locked in a dilapidated house, essentially auctioned off by her father to a disgusting older man eagerly awaiting her 20th birthday, finds a way to sexually torment her Daddy by flirting openly with a rakish, dark-skinned man. The kind of perverted scenario that could only be dreamed up by a brilliant, perverted gay man (Tennessee Williams).

Eli Wallach's casting as said rakish man (Sicilian in this case: Wallach was Jewish, but the two ethnicities could be fairly swapped out at this time) adds a puzzling charge to this movie. On the one hand his character is fairly repulsive. I doubt any 19 year-olds picture that face and that mustache when imagining a man who will save them. Wallach played The Ugly in The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly just 10 years later, of course.

But his strange looks and demeanor also make the movie so strange and wonderful. For his chemistry with Caroll Baker is undeniable and demented, especially in the very Tennesse Williams climax, complete with maniacal laughter, cuckolding, and long monologues delivered in Southern accents. The overall impression after watching it: good, but what a dirty picture.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Suspiria, 2018 - ★★★
item.description:
The bad thing about having a signature style is that attempts to branch out rarely end well. Luca Guadagnino, our poet of yearning, sensualism, and gentle desire, tries in his remake of Suspiria to make a cold, historically informed, gonzo horror film. With his level of talent and ambition he doesn’t exactly make a stinker, and he certainly does not try to ape the original. But to compare: the first Suspiria had a humming energy and taut intensity, wrapped up in 90 minutes. This version goes on long tangents about the Red Army Faction and uninspired Holocaust storylines while stretching over 3 long hours. The original probably had worse acting overall (it was giallo), but this one has Dakota Johnson, never a good sign.

The best scenes turn Guadagnino's sensitivity to the human body, usually reserved for love, into visceral disgust. The witches' dances all hit hard, especially the blood-spattered ending. But that scene was not, in fact, the ending. It kept going for 20 minutes, and that is the problem with this Suspiria. It feels like a labored attempt at a masterpiece, an attempt at cold, Germanic philosophy from a warm, Italian filmmaker. There is little to love here: it was made to be admired.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Weapons, 2025 - ★★★★
item.description:
Weapons shows just how far some energy can take you. When people say it "feels fresh" I don't think they are referring to any individual plot or story elements, none of which are exactly new. The freshness refers to the energy of the filmmaking, the feeling that every scene was made with care to get a scare. For all the highs of the last decade of "elevated horror," it did give plenty of mediocre filmmakers an excuse to make tedious, flabby, dull films (see Lamb for exhibit A). Zach Cregger, as in Barbarian, does not phone it in here.

For this reason I overlooked the structurally unsound plot, riddled with more holes than a Baltimore-area bridge. I didn’t even mind some of the more shameless jump scares, or the fact that clowns once again show up in horror. The humor and pacing, especially when following the teacher and the junkie, won me over. And it managed the rare feat of being set in recognizable Middle America and seeming to say something about it without preaching. (For all the evidence that it's "about" school shootings, it seems more clearly to deal with the children of addicts, which affects many more people than mass shootings.) Most of all it was very scary, even when the scares were very telegraphed. Sometimes the freshest approach is to play the old hits.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Hairspray, 1988 - ★★★★
item.description: Somehow John Waters achieved camp nirvana, the purest expression of his sensibility, with a PG-rated musical. No need for chicken murder or asshole gaping. For all the shock value, Pink Flamingos was really a silly, subversive movie with a soundtrack of 60s pop music--and so is Hairspray. The mean-spiritedness of Pink Flamingos is turned towards satire, and Waters' heart, always attuned to the freaks and weirdos of the world, gets to shine through without the need for attention-grabbing gimmicks. He proved he could make his style work even with a big budget, proper 35 mm film, and actual sets. Divine, as always, stars, but this time gets to try out some proper acting. As an arch-conservative philistine who simply can't understand the hip avant-garde, I like my movies to bear some semblance of narrative and emotion, and I found Hairspray to be a delight.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Cloud, 2024 - ★★★
item.description:
Cloud has an absolutely terrific concept. When explained on Internet forums, it sounds prescient and timely: an online reseller accustomed to casual, anonymous cruelty suddenly finds inexplicable karma, come to punish him for his dropshipping sins. A manifesto for the screwed-over customers of the Internet to stop sending in toothless help requests and complaints, to pick up a shotgun instead. How excited I was to hear that Kiyoshi Kurosawa, the great chronicler of modern dread, was coming out with an Internet-themed thriller, to follow up where he left off with Pulse 20 years ago.

Yet the actual execution falls flat. A soporific, thrill-less, and humorless first half (you really do watch him click stuff on his website) leads into a nonsensical shoot-'em-up finale where our doomed reseller is saved by his assistant, who just happens to be Yakuza. If this is meant to be funny, then I am yet another victim of the Japanese humor bubble, which prevents me from appreciating jokes that do not take the form of people getting hit in the balls. (Shout-out to Takeshi's Castle.) Is the action high-quality? Technically, yes. Like most contemporary shooting finales, though, it feels like a video game. There is none of the soul of 90s-era Hong Kong films, which elevated gun battles to art. Perhaps it is all too online for me. Or perhaps it is an attempt to add some excitement to the dull experience of Being Online. I think Cloud works better as a meme or Wikipedia plot description or Substack grist than as a film.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Beyond the Black Rainbow, 2010 - ★★★★
item.description:
Beyond the Black Rainbow anticipated the future course of horror more than any other movie of its time. Watching it, I noticed the slow build-up of tension beloved by elevated horror, the preoccupation with 50s and 60s era conspiracies that rule a lot of the current leftist Internet (today MKUltra is the go-to reference for an entire generation), and a revulsion with the smooth, Apple-like lines of our ongoing Silicon Valley apocalypse. All this for a movie from 2010. As the iPhone created the conditions for the 2010s, this movie anticipated the horror that would come in the 2010s. It even presaged the neon lighting that dominates movies today, which we usually attribute to Nicholas Winding-Refn and Sam Levinson but which shows up here before most mainstream examples.

Panos Cosmatos directed a film of great originality and precious little plot. For all its vision, so much is left unsaid that I found myself struggling with the cryptic narrative. What are the Sentionauts? Does the doctor have powers too, or is he trying to steal them from Elena? The ending, on the other hand, is not cryptic enough: after all that intense build-up, the ultimate fate of Dr. Barry Nyle is more Three Stooges than Lost Highway. But for these flaws, it would be a perfect successor to Lynch's mind-screw. Cosmatos sheared off all the typical elements of film that we find transfixing--plot, character, pacing--and went straight for psychedelic hypnotism. Many would imitate him.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Grey Gardens, 1975 - ★★★★
item.description:
The Beales, products of the genteel WASPs of the early 20th century, were decades ahead of their time. Jackie Kennedy was appalled at her cousin's disgusting house, at the squalor in which she lived alongside her mother, and at how far they had fallen. But Jackie was the one who represented a dying culture; it was Jackie who outlived two husbands. Edith Beale, for all her eccentricities, was a visionary eccentric. She invited in a camera crew to record her life, and joyfully performed for the camera. In 1975 this was not only unusual but seen as possibly immoral. Certainly Jackie Kennedy wouldn't let cameras catch her opining about her mother's lack of sexual fulfillment: genteel Jackie spoke with a trained voice to the cameras.

In 2025, the unfiltered confessions of Edith Beale make her far more of an icon to the young than Jackie. Today, the Beales stand first in a long lineage of reality stars, fame whores, and over-sharers that dominates our culture. The Beales won. Jackie lost.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: 28 Days Later, 2002 - ★★★
item.description:
I should have waited until 2030 to watch this movie...surely a revelation at the time, when George Romero still ruled the zombie genre. Even now, its resolutely bleak view of humanity (a trademark of Alex Garland, who would go on to bigger and better things) gives it a distinctive grunge factor. But I cannot get past the resolute ugliness of this film. In 2002 digital videography was still in its infancy: this experiment to give the film a cinema-verite immediacy was, in my eyes, a failure. All the more so because of its big-budget credentials: this is no indie flick, but a horror movie with stars of today like Cillian Murphy, Naomie Harris, and Brendan Gleeson. The coda, shot on gorgeous film, only draws more attention to the hideous digital grain.

Before that it loses interest in the zombies altogether, instead focusing on the battle between the survivors. Ever since "Night of the Living Dead", zombie movies have hinged on good and bad survivors. The idea that maybe you shouldn't kill what might be the only other humans on Earth never occurs to the characters. So we end with a great big shoot-em-up, which barrels towards an inevitable, pessimistic ending that the film then swiftly avoids. That coda may look pretty, but it is totally incongruous with the rest of the film. But then there was always artificiality under the gritty surface: how can the zombies survive for days and days? What do they eat, if not brains? And how do they survive in an empty London? As the cultural phenomenon that started the zombie craze of the 2010s, it is thrilling. 23 years later, it is also a bit phony.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Anyone But You, 2023 - ★★★½
item.description:
I don't care who knows it: Glen Powell is great. The man has charisma. In Hit Man he absolutely shined with a co-star who matched his energy. Sydney Sweeney, the ostensible star of Anyone But You, drags down the proceedings with an unconvincing snarky girl routine. But Glen Powell, Atlas-like, lifts this movie beyond what it should be. Watching this, I am reminded of Umberto Eco's quip about Casablanca, that "two cliches make us laugh. A hundred cliches move us." This movie is based on Shakespeare--just like all those 90s romcoms! It references 90s and 2000s crowdpleasers like Titanic and "Unwritten." For me it transcends cheesiness to reach a cliche nirvana, a kind of In-N-Out of big-budget romcoms.

For all the people who say "they don't make them like they used to," here you go. This is how they used to make them. They were not churning out Annie Hall and Moonstruck by the dozens when I was a child in the 2000s: this is what Hollywood used to make. That ending? A big romantic gesture for the ages. As for the time and place, it makes minor gestures towards the times (with mercifully few pronoun/zoomer jokes). It exists in the same universe as the Wedding Planner and She's the Man. Welcome back to rom com land. Your table is ready: Glen Powell will be your waiter today.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Drowning by Numbers, 1988 - ★★★★★
item.description:
Peter Greenaway is the great forgotten auteur of 20th century cinema. I have met passionate devotees of other specific niche directors--Bela Tarr, Shinya Tsukamoto, Jim Jarmusch. But while plenty have seen The Cook, the Thief, His Wife, and Her Lover, they usually stop there. Greenaway's other films, such as Drowning by Numbers, are utterly obscure. Why?

He seems the perfect director for our age. More than Kubrick he depicts the nastier side of life with utter amusement. More than Tarantino he immerses his films in references. More than Yorgos Lanthimos he plays with artificiality, turning movies into games. More than Wes Anderson he arranges painterly compositions--and while Wes simplifies his frames with geometric shapes like boxes, Greenaway fills his frames to the brim with bodies, food, trash, light, and depth. If you view cinema as an empathy machine, Greenaway clearly doesn't offer much. His male characters in particular are usually disgusting boors. But if you want to see form pushed in a wholly unique way while still being visually pleasing, then he is as exciting as it gets.

Drowning by Numbers offers one of the most delightful puzzle boxes of a movie I have ever seen. The ongoing game with numbers adds lively interest to every scene. I never once felt the pacing lag. While his static shots, lengthy narrations, and repetitive plot elements might bore some, I found it all hilarious and fascinating. Every shot is such a feast for the eyes that I never found it dull--and the repeated drownings by the three Cissie Colpitts actually became funnier as time went on. Even then, at the end, this mostly irreverent movie turns on the incredible Michael Nyman-written, Mozart-inspired score and goes for some real emotion. It works. This messy movie, Greenaway's masterpiece, can do it all: humor, beauty, disgust, pathos. This film of the proud avant-garde struck out so far into its own unexplored territory that no one else has ever bothered to even follow up, 40 years later. I wish more would follow in Greenaway's footsteps.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Under the Tuscan Sun, 2003 - ★★½
item.description:
Before Eat Pray Love, the Italian industrial complex was burnished to a sheen for yuppie Americans by Under the Tuscan Sun. A middle-aged author is blindsided by cheating, divorce, and a funny settlement where she has to supply alimony to her deadbeat writer husband. Her life in shambles, she discovers the worst part of all: she can no longer write. One gay guided tour to Italy later, and she has bought a crumbling villa. Why? She tries to latch onto the superstitions of an elderly nonna, and convince herself that signs are speaking to her. In fact, she is consuming the ambitions, beliefs, and journeys of others, remixing them in the hopes that it will spur on her creativity. All writers are vultures, and Frances Mayes has to flap down in Tuscany to find appropriate refuse. Look no further than the fact that she does not actually fix up the old house herself. Only an American would view paying other people to renovate a house as her great adventure of self-discovery.

She finds a group of eccentrics: Polish construction workers, a bipolar British woman, an Italian man very confused by her approach to courting. Fortunately, though, the movie actually ends with a moment of self-awareness. She yields the spotlight to other, more interesting characters. The whole experience leaves your mind almost instantly. The cinematography, while way ahead of the harsh LED lighting of today, doesn't live up to the standard you expect from the poster. It is pretty standard Olive Garden fare, nothing approaching the gorgeous dappled sunlight of The Talented Mr. Ripley. Many praise Diane Lane as the lead, but I found the true bright spot to be Sandra Oh, playing her best friend. Juggling a child and her own failed relationship, Oh brings some soul to a character in a movie searching for "authenticity." Had Frances Mayes focused the film on Oh's character, this might have been quite the charming romcom. If only writers would just observe, and write themselves out of their own stories entirely.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Flow, 2024 - ★★★
item.description: The little movie that could. For me, it couldn't. As an indie filmmaker I am cheered by stories like Flow: made in Blender, funded by state grants in the tiny nation of Latvia. If I'm judging films by the standards of film festivals, I heartily endorse it. Out in the wild world, I found it difficult to hold my attention. The animation is primitive, obviously, but if there is a great story then you can watch anything. But there isn't much of a story either. And those animals...something that kept bugging me was their uncanny valley of behavior, somewhere between anthropomorphized cartoon animals and real, wild animals. There is no animal savagery or instinct: they are all like very smart pets. And nothing about this flood is ever explained so all their behavior was completely arbitrary in any case. And what is it about? Survival? Teamwork? There wasn't much of substance to grasp onto, and with the low-cost animation, there isn't much style either. The great exception was the score, which did impress me. Again, Flow is a wonderful feel-good story, but once the Academy Awards start flowing in you must judge it as a real movie.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Kill the Jockey, 2024 - ★★
item.description:
We need to STOP normalizing boring-ass movies as artistic or elevated. Putting your fucking subject in the middle of every frame and holding every shot for 5 seconds longer than necessary is NOT some rebellious statement against frenetic popcorn movie editing. I am so tired of movies like Kill the Jockey that say nothing, feature no real people, and lean on tired prestige tropes to cover up its paper-thin filmmaking.

I am also tired of movies featuring listless alcoholics as protagonists, as if it is so interesting to see someone drink fake liquor on screen. I know this movie is Argentine but it just reeks of the vaguely European ennui that has infected other movies from that continent like La Chimera and Vermiglio. Why don't more filmmakers have the daring and verve of someone like Julia Ducournau, or the subtle grace of a Celine Sciamma? Oh, it's because what they do is hard, and with the right budget, Kill the Jockey is easy. They shit them out at festivals every year. Bring back amphetamines in the film industry, I can't handle these SSRI movies anymore.
item.dc:creator: Sam

item.title: Pride & Prejudice, 2005 - ★★★½
item.description:
Subtler than Bridgerton, but still a similarly successful example of adapting period romance for modern sensibilities. Lizzie is a charismatic romcom star; Mr Bennet is a warm father figure; Mrs. Bennet is just a little neurotic. No sharp social satire here, but the charm factor is enormous enough to make up for it. Compared to other period pieces, I appreciated the more restrained costuming and production of this Pride and Prejudice. The Bennets are minor country gentry, so much of the film takes place in somewhat modest homes and farms. (Of course, the English countryside has its own pastoral appeal.)

Inevitably certain aspects are rushed or cut, notably the subplot with Lydia and Mr. Wickham. But the subplot with Jane and Bingley is a highlight, maybe even better than the main storyline. The young Rosamund Pike was one of the most luminous people to ever live. I haven't seen the 1995 BBC version, though I imagine a miniseries would be best to do the novel justice. This version just about threads the needle right between daring and traditional.

item.title: Rollerball, 1975 - ★★★
item.description:
ROLLERBALL. Fuck, I want to play some ROLLERBALL. This fictional game is so exciting, so lawless, so generally awesome that not only does it credibly serve as the central entertainment for a future society, it was actually played by the crew between takes on set. Promoters contacted Norman Jewison about forming ROLLERBALL leagues. Jewison was outraged, but I honestly think America might be better off if we started playing ROLLERBALL in the 70s instead of the NFL. After all, ROLLERBALL is intended to discourage individualism: quaint that they thought collectivism would

The ROLLERBALL scenes are so kinetic that they almost compensate for the rest of the film, which curiously drags. I literally started to doze off in the theater between ROLLERBALL sequences. Still, any time I can see a conspiratorial 70s sci-fi movie, I'm pleased. James Caan also just looks like a 70s pro athlete. Our current crop of tough-guy actors are woefully lacking in comparison. Caan's character is quite dull, but when he and the rest of the cast stop talking and put on the roller skates, this movie sings.

item.title: Mamma Mia!, 2008 - ★★★
item.description:
Mamma Mia: a cautionary tale about the boundless self-indulgence of boomers. The 70s were just BETTER, and every moment since then should be dedicated to shameless nostalgia. Amanda Seyfried may be the one getting married, but come on, wide-eyed millennial. Your dreams are a pale shadow of your mom's pre-AIDS sexual adventures; your man (named Sky, not even a real name) is a sideshow to your three (still-vigorous) possible daddies. Your wedding is really about your mother. This world was, and has always been, a vehicle for Americans born between 1945 and 1964 to find themselves. Meryl Streep may not sing well, but she fucked three men in a month and then ran a hotel in Greece, somehow winning over the presumably conservative rural Greek islanders despite her swinging, Bohemian lifestyle. What is holy matrimony compared to sweaty European bodies at a disco, bouncing to Gimme Gimme Gimme a Man After Midnight?

A lot of people find this movie comforting. It made me rather anxious, especially when the three Dynamos start a hellcat rendition of Dancing Queen, their eyes popping from old-people amphetamines. I did not find Pierce Brosnan's singing comforting either, instead fast-forwarding through all his slow duets with Meryl. If I was as sauced up watching this as all the actors were while filming it, I could build up some resistance to its near-lethal dose of theater kid energy. Sober as I was, I had to sit and watch like the grumpy guy at a Cancun karaoke, smiling through my teeth as all the white ladies sang and pointed and took Jello shots.

item.title: Merrily We Go to Hell, 1932 - ★★
item.description:
In theory you can never run out of stories about unhappy marriages. In the case of Merrily We Go To Hell, I think I've seen this one a few times already. Fredric March plays a truly pathetic alcoholic writer, and Sylvia Sidney is the woman who thinks he is great. Maybe she is the pathetic one. They try a "modern marriage," an ideal which has entrapped the exact same kind of people in the exact same disastrous experiments for 100 years running, and it goes as well as any bourgeois marriage described in the Modern Love column.

The script is definitely second-rate, zinger-wise, compared to the great screwballs and romcoms of the era. Hanging out with these characters makes you feel like you got invited to the wrong New York City party. Didn't someone say Ernst Lubitsch was coming? Where is Howard Hawks? Can someone get Barbara Stanwyck on the phone? Oh, Cary Grant is here, but he left after 5 minutes. At least the party is short, and you get to go home after less than 90 minutes.

item.title: Mickey 17, 2025 - ★★½
item.description:
Mickey 17 is a case study for how a good concept and skilled direction can be totally sunk by bad characters. There is so much satirical potential locked up in that expandable cloning premise, and Bong Joon-Ho is just the man to take it on with a big sci-fi budget. But his other films all had memorable, or at least realistic, characters. (Even Snowpiercer, the closest analogue to Mickey 17, had some good ones.) Here we have an intentionally annoying loser, a generic You Go Girl, a bad Trump impression, and some ugly aliens. Steven Yeun alone brings some pizzazz to his character, but he gets about 10 minutes of screentime.

That concept, too, gets lost in a muddle about the ugly aliens. I don't care about ugly aliens. I did care about the original clone Mickey 17 and his sinister clone Mickey 18 possibly getting killed, but this gets subsumed into the squabble over the ugly aliens. What about other Expendables? Are there some with the intelligence to think about what it means to die over and over? All this is sidelined in favor of these ugly fucking aliens. What seemed like brainy science fiction turned out to be brainless.

item.title: Northern Lights, 1978 - ★★★★
item.description:
North Dakota: cold, remote, Scandinavian, and very far from the film industry. The 1970s saw socially conscious filmmakers fan out around the globe in search of untold stories, but surely no one before or since has focused on populist organizers in the Upper Midwest of the 1910s. There is a Bergmanian embrace of stark visuals and richly illuminated faces in black-and-white, but a distinctly American spirit of optimism and defiance. Rob Nilsson treats his subject with great tenderness, especially in a lovely scene involving two lovers courting in a barn.

This tenderness does undercut the effectiveness of Northern Lights as a polemical film: it never displays poverty, the politicians who organize against the Non-Partisan League, or indeed any enemy at all. We must simply believe in the righteousness of the cause, told through voiceover, instead of seeing its urgent need in the form of drama. Better for it to err on the side of art instead of propaganda, though. It stands as a documentary-like look at a very chilly, now extinct form of life that most of America forgot ever existed.

item.title: Pink Flamingos, 1972 - ★★½
item.description:
You really had to be there. And by "be there," I mean "film graphic rape scenes where you crush chickens to death in 70s Baltimore but also make it funny." Seriously, I wonder how many of the softboy queer artists who enjoy John Waters's quips and fun mustache have actually seen this movie. The man has talent, but this feels a bit low-effort. Its massive success is proof that life really was easier for the boomers.

It was possibly necessary for the culture, but if you still find this funny in 2025 then you might be 14 years old, and you should also never ever complain about South Park. Even Divine recognized 15 years later that the time of Pink Flamingos had passed by declining to appear in a sequel, which presumably would have started off with eating more dogshit, progressed to horseshit, and climaxed with the entire city being submerged in a literal ocean of shit. (This actually happened in Baltimore in 1993, before it was covered up by David Simon and the liberal media.)

The key to the film is the tagline: an "exercise" in poor taste. Not a film. An exercise routine. An act of poor taste athletics. A gross-out sports match. Impressive, if you like that stuff, but I'll stick to basketball for my displays of athletics.

item.title: Kong: Skull Island, 2017 - ★★★½
item.description: Much like X-Men First Class, Kong Skull Island extracts a lot of quality from its 70s setting. Maybe Hollywood's latent memories of that great time in filmmaking inspires them to add more flair and effort to these blockbusters. The island setting helps a lot too: instead of the same ol' CGI city destruction, you get a more focused assault on a small team, plus some classic adventure-story "struggle to survive" storylines. I liked this probably more than I should have. I liked John C. Reilly a lot, and wish he was in more movies. The storyline is pretty standard for these things (evil humans want to kill Kong even though he's the only one who can save us from the real monsters), but it threads the needle in terms of ironic camp and genuine emotion. I'll take it over almost any superhero flick.
